derived_full_section.heading: Standardizing pre-training corpus for accurate transcriptomic profiling
derived_full_section.text:
To create a comprehensive pre-trained corpus, we included 36.77 million human single-cell transcriptomes from various publicly available datasets. We focused on droplet-based sequencing techniques to ensure consistency in expression value metrics. We filtered potential doublets and retained cells with both total reads and mitochondrial reads laying within a 3-standard-deviation margin of the average values for each measurement within that particular dataset. Cells with elevated mutational loads were carefully excluded to maintain data integrity [ [17](#B17) ] and prevent potential misinterpretations arising from substantial network rewiring that can not be detected by genome sequencing [ [18](#B18) ]. Only Ensembl-annotated protein-coding/microRNA genes were kept for downstream processing. Cells expressing fewer than seven detected genes were excluded from the analysis since the 15% masking strategy used during pre-training was unable to effectively obscure individual genes in cells with reduced transcriptional detection [ [19](#B19) ]. Ultimately, a total of 34.2 million cells from 7225 samples met the defined filtration criteria and were included for further analysis. These cells were compiled and stored in .loom HDF5 format, accompanied by metadata extracted from the original studies.

To represent the transcriptome of each single cell non-parametrically, we followed instructions of the rank value encoding method [ [7](#B7) ]. Briefly, this method prioritized genes distinguishing cellular states via ratings normalized throughout the corpus, thereby highlighting transcription factors expressed at lower levels while attenuating genes that are universally expressed. The specific steps involved calculating the nonzero median expression for each detected gene across all cells and then normalizing the gene expression against total read counts of the sample and its corresponding nonzero median. This yielded the normalized expression values. Finally, we ranked the normalized expression values of each cell to obtain rank values. Tokenization of encodings made use of a 23 698-gene vocabulary. The Huggingface Datasets, which offers computational efficiency and facilitates archiving, was utilized to store our data.

Introduction
Despite these advances, several challenges remain. First, current models often struggle to fully denoise technical noise, such as batch effects introduced by different platforms, protocols, or labs. Most efforts to address this rely on input-level preprocessing rather than integrating noise-aware mechanisms within model architectures. Second, while diffusion models have shown impressive denoising capabilities in protein design [
[16](#B16)
], they are rarely adopted in single-cell transcriptomics, despite their natural advantage in mitigating noise and heterogeneity that are pervasive in single-cell data. Third, relatively few foundation models are equipped to integrate multi-modal data, such as jointly modeling scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics, limiting their utility in reconstructing tissue-level organization and dynamics.
To address these challenges, we present scDifformer, a diffusion-augmented transformer model enhanced with a diffusion-driven post-training phase designed to improve the fidelity and generalizability of virtual cell representations. Trained on a corpus of 34.2 million human single-cell transcriptomes spanning diverse tissues and biological conditions, scDifformer captures rich context-aware gene expression patterns while actively denoising technical variation through a discrete diffusion module. A second training stage, absent in most existing frameworks, enables the model to recover clean, biologically meaningful signals from sparse and heterogeneous data. In addition to accurate cell type annotation, scDifformer also enables the robust integration of immune cells from multiple organs and accurately captures gene- and pathway-level differences. Notably, applied to real-world data, it reconstructs canonical hematopoietic trajectories from hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to terminal immune lineages across diverse tissues, including bone marrow, spleen, thymus, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). We further demonstrate its potential usage in spatial transcriptomic data analysis, by integrating it with a graph neural network, GraphSAGE, to perform spot-level deconvolution. This approach offers a promising direction for unifying single-cell and spatial information within a shared modeling framework. These results highlight scDifformer as a scalable, biologically grounded framework capable of unifying single-cell information, and advancing the construction of high-fidelity, multi-modal virtual cell models.

derived_full_section.heading: Introduction
derived_full_section.text:
The concept of a virtual cell was proposed decades ago as a framework to understand cell behavior and transitions over time [ [1](#B1) ]. It is a computational representation that captures the dynamic interactions and regulatory processes of all DNA, RNA, proteins, and metabolites within a cell. Early efforts toward building virtual cells relied on systems of ordinary differential equations to model cellular networks [ [2](#B2) ]. However, the inherent complexity of intracellular processes and the lack of high-resolution molecular data limited the feasibility of these approaches. The advent of next-generation sequencing technologies, such as single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST), has revolutionized our ability to profile cells across tissues, conditions, and developmental stages. These technologies have generated massive, high-dimensional datasets that capture cellular heterogeneity and dynamics with unprecedented resolution [ [3](#B3) ]. Concurrently, advances in deep learning, particularly natural language models [ [4](#B4) ], have enabled the development of scalable, data-driven models that can extract meaningful biological representations from these complex datasets. Together, these innovations have laid the foundation for constructing virtual cell models that are both comprehensive and generalizable.

A major recent direction in this effort involves the development of cell foundation models, which are large-scale pretrained models designed to learn universal representations of single-cell transcriptomes. Most existing models adopt transformer-based architectures, inspired by advances in natural language processing (NLP) and biological sequence modeling, whereas Saturn [ [5](#B5) ] and SCimilarity [ [6](#B6) ] employ alternative architecture. Geneformer [ [7](#B7) ], GeneCompass [ [8](#B8) ], and scBERT [ [9](#B9) ] leverage masked language modeling (MLM) on rank- or token-based gene expression encodings to learn contextual embeddings. These models show strong performance on tasks such as cell type classification, though they often rely heavily on input normalization schemes to control for batch effects and sparsity. Other approaches emphasize architectural advances. Models such as scGPT [ [10](#B10) ], CellFM [ [11](#B11) ], scFoundation [ [12](#B12) ], and xTrimoGene [ [13](#B13) ] treat full expression profiles as sparse sequences, using attention mechanisms or state-space models to capture complex gene-cell dependencies. These architectures support a wide range of downstream applications, from transfer learning to perturbation response prediction, and can be trained at a massive scale. A third emerging direction focuses on cross-species generalization, with models like Universal Cell Embedding [ [14](#B14) ] and TranscriptFormer [ [15](#B15) ] aiming to learn foundational representations that transfer across species boundaries, an essential step toward virtual cell modeling in evolutionary and comparative biology.

Despite these advances, several challenges remain. First, current models often struggle to fully denoise technical noise, such as batch effects introduced by different platforms, protocols, or labs. Most efforts to address this rely on input-level preprocessing rather than integrating noise-aware mechanisms within model architectures. Second, while diffusion models have shown impressive denoising capabilities in protein design [ [16](#B16) ], they are rarely adopted in single-cell transcriptomics, despite their natural advantage in mitigating noise and heterogeneity that are pervasive in single-cell data. Third, relatively few foundation models are equipped to integrate multi-modal data, such as jointly modeling scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics, limiting their utility in reconstructing tissue-level organization and dynamics.

To address these challenges, we present scDifformer, a diffusion-augmented transformer model enhanced with a diffusion-driven post-training phase designed to improve the fidelity and generalizability of virtual cell representations. Trained on a corpus of 34.2 million human single-cell transcriptomes spanning diverse tissues and biological conditions, scDifformer captures rich context-aware gene expression patterns while actively denoising technical variation through a discrete diffusion module. A second training stage, absent in most existing frameworks, enables the model to recover clean, biologically meaningful signals from sparse and heterogeneous data. In addition to accurate cell type annotation, scDifformer also enables the robust integration of immune cells from multiple organs and accurately captures gene- and pathway-level differences. Notably, applied to real-world data, it reconstructs canonical hematopoietic trajectories from hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to terminal immune lineages across diverse tissues, including bone marrow, spleen, thymus, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). We further demonstrate its potential usage in spatial transcriptomic data analysis, by integrating it with a graph neural network, GraphSAGE, to perform spot-level deconvolution. This approach offers a promising direction for unifying single-cell and spatial information within a shared modeling framework. These results highlight scDifformer as a scalable, biologically grounded framework capable of unifying single-cell information, and advancing the construction of high-fidelity, multi-modal virtual cell models.

data_source_chunks.heading: Discussion
data_source_chunks.text:
scDifformer: diffusion-based post-training for virtual cell modeling across large-scale single-cell data
Discussion
In this study, we developed scDifformer, a large-scale single-cell foundation model that integrates the transformer-based architecture of Geneformer with a diffusion probabilistic module via a novel post-training step. Leveraging an extensive pre-training corpus of 34.2 million human single-cell transcriptomes from publicly available databases including DISCO and CZ CELLxGENE, scDifformer surpasses existing models such as scBERT and Geneformer, both in scale and downstream annotation performance. The diffusion-enhanced architecture effectively reduces data-driven noise, refines learned representations, and accelerates convergence. Moreover, our attention-based interpretation revealed biologically meaningful gene signatures, linking top-ranked attention genes to enriched pathways consistent with known cell identities. Additionally, extending scDifformer embeddings to spatial transcriptomics through integration with the GraphSAGE graph neural network demonstrated superior performance in simulated spot-level deconvolution tasks. This innovative step represents the first successful application of diffusion modeling in spatial transcriptomics, suggesting a promising strategy for future integration of spatial and single-cell data.
Despite these advances, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, our current dataset primarily includes normal or steady-state cellular profiles, with limited representation of abnormal, perturbed, or disease-associated cells. This restricts the model's predictive capacity in pathological conditions, limiting its immediate applicability in areas such as disease modeling or therapeutic perturbation studies. Second, while our cross-tissue analysis validated performance using immune cells, a relatively well-defined cellular population, future studies should investigate more complex developmental processes, such as embryonic development or stem-cell differentiation pathways. Modeling these processes could substantially impact developmental biology and regenerative medicine, including advancements in artificial organ technologies. Third, although we demonstrated potential for integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data, scDifformer is not inherently a multi-modal model. Comprehensive multi-modal frameworks should integrate additional data types, such as proteomics, epigenomics, and metabolomics, to fully capture cellular complexity and interactions at multiple molecular layers.
Addressing these limitations will guide our future research efforts. One critical direction is to expand training datasets to encompass diverse abnormal or perturbed cellular states, enhancing the model's ability to capture disease progression, cellular response to treatments, and dynamic reprogramming events. Additionally, the development of fully multi-modal foundation models, capable of jointly embedding transcriptomic, proteomic, and other molecular data, represents an exciting avenue to build next-generation virtual cells. Such models would offer deeper insights into cellular function and regulation, significantly advancing our capability to reconstruct accurate, context-aware biological simulations.

derived_full_section.heading: Construction of the training corpus
derived_full_section.text: To construct a comprehensive and high-quality corpus for pre-training, we compiled a total of 34.2 million single cells derived from over 7000 publicly available studies, integrating data from large-scale repositories such as DISCO [ [53](#B53) ] and CZ CELLxGENE [ [54](#B54) ], representing cells from diversity tissues (Fig. [1B](#F1) ). To ensure consistency and reliability across datasets, we implemented a standardized filtering pipeline (see "Materials and methods" section). To represent the transcriptome of each cell in a way that is compatible with transformer architectures, we adopted the rank value encoding strategy, which encodes the relative expression ranks of genes rather than their absolute values (Fig. [1A](#F1) ). As previously demonstrated in Geneformer [ [7](#B7) ], rank-based encoding effectively transforms transcriptomic profiles into a language-like input sequence, enabling the model to capture contextual dependencies among genes while preserving biologically meaningful expression pattern. This encoding is well-suited to transformer architectures, as it preserves co-expression pattern while reducing sensitivity to technical variation.

However, the inherent complexity of intracellular processes and the lack of high-resolution molecular data limited the feasibility of these approaches. The advent of next-generation sequencing technologies, such as single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST), has revolutionized our ability to profile cells across tissues, conditions, and developmental stages. These technologies have generated massive, high-dimensional datasets that capture cellular heterogeneity and dynamics with unprecedented resolution [ [3](#B3) ]. Concurrently, advances in deep learning, particularly natural language models [ [4](#B4) ], have enabled the development of scalable, data-driven models that can extract meaningful biological representations from these complex datasets. Together, these innovations have laid the foundation for constructing virtual cell models that are both comprehensive and generalizable.

A major recent direction in this effort involves the development of cell foundation models, which are large-scale pretrained models designed to learn universal representations of single-cell transcriptomes. Most existing models adopt transformer-based architectures, inspired by advances in natural language processing (NLP) and biological sequence modeling, whereas Saturn [ [5](#B5) ] and SCimilarity [ [6](#B6) ] employ alternative architecture. Geneformer [ [7](#B7) ], GeneCompass [ [8](#B8) ], and scBERT [ [9](#B9) ] leverage masked language modeling (MLM) on rank- or token-based gene expression encodings to learn contextual embeddings. These models show strong performance on tasks such as cell type classification, though they often rely heavily on input normalization schemes to control for batch effects and sparsity. Other approaches emphasize architectural advances. Models such as scGPT [ [10](#B10) ], CellFM [ [11](#B11) ], scFoundation [ [12](#B12) ], and xTrimoGene [ [13](#B13) ] treat full expression profiles as sparse sequences, using attention mechanisms or state-space models to capture complex gene-cell dependencies. These architectures support a wide range of downstream applications, from transfer learning to perturbation response prediction, and can be trained at a massive scale. A third emerging direction focuses on cross-species generalization, with models like Universal Cell Embedding [ [14](#B14) ] and TranscriptFormer [ [15](#B15) ] aiming to learn foundational representations that transfer across species boundaries, an essential step toward virtual cell modeling in evolutionary and comparative biology.

Despite these advances, several challenges remain. First, current models often struggle to fully denoise technical noise, such as batch effects introduced by different platforms, protocols, or labs. Most efforts to address this rely on input-level preprocessing rather than integrating noise-aware mechanisms within model architectures. Second, while diffusion models have shown impressive denoising capabilities in protein design [ [16](#B16) ], they are rarely adopted in single-cell transcriptomics, despite their natural advantage in mitigating noise and heterogeneity that are pervasive in single-cell data. Third, relatively few foundation models are equipped to integrate multi-modal data, such as jointly modeling scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics, limiting their utility in reconstructing tissue-level organization and dynamics.

To address these challenges, we present scDifformer, a diffusion-augmented transformer model enhanced with a diffusion-driven post-training phase designed to improve the fidelity and generalizability of virtual cell representations. Trained on a corpus of 34.2 million human single-cell transcriptomes spanning diverse tissues and biological conditions, scDifformer captures rich context-aware gene expression patterns while actively denoising technical variation through a discrete diffusion module. A second training stage, absent in most existing frameworks, enables the model to recover clean, biologically meaningful signals from sparse and heterogeneous data. In addition to accurate cell type annotation, scDifformer also enables the robust integration of immune cells from multiple organs and accurately captures gene- and pathway-level differences. Notably, applied to real-world data, it reconstructs canonical hematopoietic trajectories from hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to terminal immune lineages across diverse tissues, including bone marrow, spleen, thymus, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). We further demonstrate its potential usage in spatial transcriptomic data analysis, by integrating it with a graph neural network, GraphSAGE, to perform spot-level deconvolution. This approach offers a promising direction for unifying single-cell and spatial information within a shared modeling framework. These results highlight scDifformer as a scalable, biologically grounded framework capable of unifying single-cell information, and advancing the construction of high-fidelity, multi-modal virtual cell models.

data_source_sections.heading: Discussion
data_source_sections.text:
In this study, we developed scDifformer, a large-scale single-cell foundation model that integrates the transformer-based architecture of Geneformer with a diffusion probabilistic module via a novel post-training step. Leveraging an extensive pre-training corpus of 34.2 million human single-cell transcriptomes from publicly available databases including DISCO and CZ CELLxGENE, scDifformer surpasses existing models such as scBERT and Geneformer, both in scale and downstream annotation performance. The diffusion-enhanced architecture effectively reduces data-driven noise, refines learned representations, and accelerates convergence. Moreover, our attention-based interpretation revealed biologically meaningful gene signatures, linking top-ranked attention genes to enriched pathways consistent with known cell identities. Additionally, extending scDifformer embeddings to spatial transcriptomics through integration with the GraphSAGE graph neural network demonstrated superior performance in simulated spot-level deconvolution tasks. This innovative step represents the first successful application of diffusion modeling in spatial transcriptomics, suggesting a promising strategy for future integration of spatial and single-cell data.

Despite these advances, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, our current dataset primarily includes normal or steady-state cellular profiles, with limited representation of abnormal, perturbed, or disease-associated cells. This restricts the model's predictive capacity in pathological conditions, limiting its immediate applicability in areas such as disease modeling or therapeutic perturbation studies. Second, while our cross-tissue analysis validated performance using immune cells, a relatively well-defined cellular population, future studies should investigate more complex developmental processes, such as embryonic development or stem-cell differentiation pathways. Modeling these processes could substantially impact developmental biology and regenerative medicine, including advancements in artificial organ technologies. Third, although we demonstrated potential for integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data, scDifformer is not inherently a multi-modal model. Comprehensive multi-modal frameworks should integrate additional data types, such as proteomics, epigenomics, and metabolomics, to fully capture cellular complexity and interactions at multiple molecular layers.

Addressing these limitations will guide our future research efforts. One critical direction is to expand training datasets to encompass diverse abnormal or perturbed cellular states, enhancing the model's ability to capture disease progression, cellular response to treatments, and dynamic reprogramming events. Additionally, the development of fully multi-modal foundation models, capable of jointly embedding transcriptomic, proteomic, and other molecular data, represents an exciting avenue to build next-generation virtual cells. Such models would offer deeper insights into cellular function and regulation, significantly advancing our capability to reconstruct accurate, context-aware biological simulations.

input_representation_sections.heading: Standardizing pre-training corpus for accurate transcriptomic profiling
input_representation_sections.text:
To create a comprehensive pre-trained corpus, we included 36.77 million human single-cell transcriptomes from various publicly available datasets. We focused on droplet-based sequencing techniques to ensure consistency in expression value metrics. We filtered potential doublets and retained cells with both total reads and mitochondrial reads laying within a 3-standard-deviation margin of the average values for each measurement within that particular dataset. Cells with elevated mutational loads were carefully excluded to maintain data integrity [ [17](#B17) ] and prevent potential misinterpretations arising from substantial network rewiring that can not be detected by genome sequencing [ [18](#B18) ]. Only Ensembl-annotated protein-coding/microRNA genes were kept for downstream processing. Cells expressing fewer than seven detected genes were excluded from the analysis since the 15% masking strategy used during pre-training was unable to effectively obscure individual genes in cells with reduced transcriptional detection [ [19](#B19) ]. Ultimately, a total of 34.2 million cells from 7225 samples met the defined filtration criteria and were included for further analysis. These cells were compiled and stored in .loom HDF5 format, accompanied by metadata extracted from the original studies.

To represent the transcriptome of each single cell non-parametrically, we followed instructions of the rank value encoding method [ [7](#B7) ]. Briefly, this method prioritized genes distinguishing cellular states via ratings normalized throughout the corpus, thereby highlighting transcription factors expressed at lower levels while attenuating genes that are universally expressed. The specific steps involved calculating the nonzero median expression for each detected gene across all cells and then normalizing the gene expression against total read counts of the sample and its corresponding nonzero median. This yielded the normalized expression values. Finally, we ranked the normalized expression values of each cell to obtain rank values. Tokenization of encodings made use of a 23 698-gene vocabulary. The Huggingface Datasets, which offers computational efficiency and facilitates archiving, was utilized to store our data.

input_representation_sections.heading: Construction of the training corpus
input_representation_sections.text: To construct a comprehensive and high-quality corpus for pre-training, we compiled a total of 34.2 million single cells derived from over 7000 publicly available studies, integrating data from large-scale repositories such as DISCO [ [53](#B53) ] and CZ CELLxGENE [ [54](#B54) ], representing cells from diversity tissues (Fig. [1B](#F1) ). To ensure consistency and reliability across datasets, we implemented a standardized filtering pipeline (see "Materials and methods" section). To represent the transcriptome of each cell in a way that is compatible with transformer architectures, we adopted the rank value encoding strategy, which encodes the relative expression ranks of genes rather than their absolute values (Fig. [1A](#F1) ). As previously demonstrated in Geneformer [ [7](#B7) ], rank-based encoding effectively transforms transcriptomic profiles into a language-like input sequence, enabling the model to capture contextual dependencies among genes while preserving biologically meaningful expression pattern. This encoding is well-suited to transformer architectures, as it preserves co-expression pattern while reducing sensitivity to technical variation.

primary_input_representation_chunk.text:
2 Related Work
Geometry of neural representations. The idea that concepts occupy linear directions dates to distributional word vectors and their analogy structure (Mikolov et al., 2013), and has been formalized for modern LLMs as the linear representation hypothesis (Park et al., 2024), with categorical and hierarchical concepts shown to form polytopes and nested subspaces (Park et al., 2025) and latent state shown to be linearly decodable in world models (Nanda et al., 2023). Superposition explains why more features than dimensions can coexist, at the cost of interference (Elhage et al., 2022), and dictionary learning / sparse autoencoders recover many such features (Cunningham et al., 2024). Complementary work characterizes the coarse geometry of the representation space itself: contextual embeddings are highly anisotropic, occupying a narrow cone (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019); hidden representations have an intrinsic dimension far below the ambient width that rises then falls with depth (Ansuini et al., 2019; Valeriani et al., 2023); and representation similarity across networks can be quantified with CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019) and SVCCA (Raghu et al., 2017). The Platonic representation hypothesis conjectures that models trained on different data converge toward a shared statistical geometry (Huh et al., 2024). We port this toolkit wholesale to biological LLMs and treat 'how linear, how low-dimensional, how convergent' as measurable quantities.
What single-cell foundation models encode. SCFMs differ in tokenization and scale-rank-value encoding in Geneformer (Theodoris et al., 2023), binned-value tokens in scGPT (Cui et al., 2024) and scBERT (Yang et al., 2022), protein-embedding gene keys in UCE (Rosen et al., 2023), and cell-as-token modeling in CellPLM (Wen et al., 2024); reviews catalog the family (Szałata et al., 2024). Independent evaluations question the payoff of this scale (Boiarsky et al., 2023; Kedzierska et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023), and a mechanistic line finds organized-but-correlational content: co-expression-dominated attention (Kendiukhov, 2026b), interpretable cell-type programs but scarce regulatory logic in sparse-autoencoder features (Kendiukhov, 2026c,d), convergent inhibitory circuits (Kendiukhov, 2026a), a low-dimensional spectral geometry of knowledge (Kendiukhov, 2026e), and an extractable, curved hematopoietic manifold (Kendiukhov, 2026f). Our study is complementary and representational: rather than tracing circuits or dictionary features, we ask whether the geometry that makes LLM knowledge legible is present, and we benchmark it against expression baselines throughout.

2 Related Work
Geometry of neural representations. The idea that concepts occupy linear directions dates to distributional word vectors and their analogy structure (Mikolov et al., 2013), and has been formalized for modern LLMs as the linear representation hypothesis (Park et al., 2024), with categorical and hierarchical concepts shown to form polytopes and nested subspaces (Park et al., 2025) and latent state shown to be linearly decodable in world models (Nanda et al., 2023). Superposition explains why more features than dimensions can coexist, at the cost of interference (Elhage et al., 2022), and dictionary learning / sparse autoencoders recover many such features (Cunningham et al., 2024). Complementary work characterizes the coarse geometry of the representation space itself: contextual embeddings are highly anisotropic, occupying a narrow cone (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019); hidden representations have an intrinsic dimension far below the ambient width that rises then falls with depth (Ansuini et al., 2019; Valeriani et al., 2023); and representation similarity across networks can be quantified with CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019) and SVCCA (Raghu et al., 2017). The Platonic representation hypothesis conjectures that models trained on different data converge toward a shared statistical geometry (Huh et al., 2024). We port this toolkit wholesale to biological LLMs and treat 'how linear, how low-dimensional, how convergent' as measurable quantities.

Two bodies of evidence suggest the answer is nuanced. First, benchmark studies repeatedly find that SCFMs offer only modest advantages over classical pipelines: logistic regression rivals scBERT and scGPT on annotation (Boiarsky et al., 2023), classical integration beats zero-shot SCFMs (Kedzierska et al., 2025), and PCA is a stubborn baseline across task suites (Liu et al., 2023). If the extra 'knowledge' were geometrically organized and readily accessible, one might expect larger gains. Second, a focused interpretability program reports that SCFM internals store organized but predominantly correlational biology occupying a lowdimensional, superposed geometry: attention captures co-expression rather than unique regulatory signal (Kendiukhov, 2026b), sparse autoencoders recover interpretable cell-type programs (Kendiukhov, 2026c) but minimal causal regulatory logic (Kendiukhov, 2026d), causal circuits are inhibition-dominated and convergent across models (Kendiukhov, 2026a), the encoded knowledge has a multi-dimensional spectral geometry (Kendiukhov, 2026e), and a curved hematopoietic manifold can be read out of scGPT to recover differentiation algorithms (Kendiukhov, 2026f). These threads motivate a direct, quantitative comparison of SCFM representational geometry against both the LLM ideal and expression-space baselines.

We provide that comparison. Using four SCFMs of widely varying scale, a curated 0 . 42 M-cell atlas panel with cell-type, tissue, sex, assay, disease, donor, and cell-cycle annotations, and a bone-marrow differentiation dataset with ground-truth pseudotime, we measure six families of geometric properties and, for every one, ask how much of the observed structure exceeds what a linear expression embedding (highly variable genes, PCA, scVI (Lopez et al., 2018)) already provides. Second, a focused interpretability program reports that SCFM internals store organized but predominantly correlational biology occupying a lowdimensional, superposed geometry: attention captures co-expression rather than unique regulatory signal (Kendiukhov, 2026b), sparse autoencoders recover interpretable cell-type programs (Kendiukhov, 2026c) but minimal causal regulatory logic (Kendiukhov, 2026d), causal circuits are inhibition-dominated and convergent across models (Kendiukhov, 2026a), the encoded knowledge has a multi-dimensional spectral geometry (Kendiukhov, 2026e), and a curved hematopoietic manifold can be read out of scGPT to recover differentiation algorithms (Kendiukhov, 2026f). These threads motivate a direct, quantitative comparison of SCFM representational geometry against both the LLM ideal and expression-space baselines.

We provide that comparison. Using four SCFMs of widely varying scale, a curated 0 . 42 M-cell atlas panel with cell-type, tissue, sex, assay, disease, donor, and cell-cycle annotations, and a bone-marrow differentiation dataset with ground-truth pseudotime, we measure six families of geometric properties and, for every one, ask how much of the observed structure exceeds what a linear expression embedding (highly variable genes, PCA, scVI (Lopez et al., 2018)) already provides. Our aim is deliberately descriptive and honest rather than method-building: we characterize what geometry is there , and we report that it is consistently more modest than the language-model literature would predict.

####### Contributions.

- We assemble a reusable evaluation suite for SCFM representational geometry that couples six analysis families-intrinsic dimension and anisotropy, linear and nonlinear probing with control tasks, concept-direction parallelism and steering, categorical/hierarchical alignment, cross-model CKA, and trajectory-manifold recovery-to matched expression baselines (Figure 1).
- We show that SCFM representations are low-dimensional and strongly anisotropic (Table 2), and that coarse categorical knowledge is linearly decodable but only marginally beyond PCA, with the largest SCFM gains on intermediate distinctions (subtype, cell type) and essentially none on sex or already-easy compartment labels (Figure 3).
- We find the linear-representation picture holds only weakly: concept directions are above-chance but far from parallel, improve under a causal whitening yet remain modest, and support steering with 54 -66% success; unrelated concepts are, encouragingly, near-orthogonal (Figure 4).
- We show developmental knowledge is curved rather than linear-a single direction captures u1D445 2 ≤ 0 . 61 of pseudotime while a geodesic reaches u1D70C ≈ 0 . 80 , matching a classical diffusion map (Figure 6)-and that cross-model geometry converges moderately with each other but weakly to a cell-ontology kernel (Figure 5).
- Throughout, we quantify the baseline-relative effect size and report negative results, giving a calibrated account of how far SCFM geometry is from the linear ideal and how much of it is genuinely model-added.

Figure 1: Analysis overview. A metadata-rich single-cell atlas panel is encoded by four frozen biological LLMs; we extract per-layer hidden states and cell embeddings and subject them to six families of geometric analysis. Every measurement is compared against linear expression baselines (highly variable genes, PCA, scVI) to isolate the structure the models actually add.

3.2 Evaluation corpus and metadata
The primary corpus is a 0 . 42 M-cell panel sampled from the CZ CELLxGENE Discover census (CZI Cell Science Program et al., 2025), which aggregates atlas resources including the Human Cell Atlas (Regev et al., 2017) and Tabula Sapiens (The Tabula Sapiens Consortium, 2022), plus Zheng PBMCs (Zheng et al., 2017). We sampled to balance tissues and assays and to retain cells carrying complete metadata for nine attributes: compartment (4 classes: immune, epithelial, stromal, endothelial), cell type (21 coarse Cell Ontology classes (Diehl et al., 2016)), subtype (58 fine classes), tissue (14), sex (2), assay (6 technologies, a batch/nuisance variable), disease (healthy vs. disease), donor (40), and cell-cycle phase (3, scored from canonical markers (Wolf et al., 2018)). Cell-type identities follow curated marker sets (Franzén et al., 2019). For trajectory analysis we use a bone-marrow CD34 + hematopoiesis dataset with ground-truth pseudotime computed by diffusion pseudotime (Haghverdi et al., 2016) and cross-checked with Palantir (Setty et al., 2019); the differentiation splits into erythroid, myeloid, and lymphoid branches.

2 Related Work
Geometry of neural representations. The idea that concepts occupy linear directions dates to distributional word vectors and their analogy structure (Mikolov et al., 2013), and has been formalized for modern LLMs as the linear representation hypothesis (Park et al., 2024), with categorical and hierarchical concepts shown to form polytopes and nested subspaces (Park et al., 2025) and latent state shown to be linearly decodable in world models (Nanda et al., 2023). Superposition explains why more features than dimensions can coexist, at the cost of interference (Elhage et al., 2022), and dictionary learning / sparse autoencoders recover many such features (Cunningham et al., 2024). Complementary work characterizes the coarse geometry of the representation space itself: contextual embeddings are highly anisotropic, occupying a narrow cone (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019); hidden representations have an intrinsic dimension far below the ambient width that rises then falls with depth (Ansuini et al., 2019; Valeriani et al., 2023); and representation similarity across networks can be quantified with CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019) and SVCCA (Raghu et al., 2017). The Platonic representation hypothesis conjectures that models trained on different data converge toward a shared statistical geometry (Huh et al., 2024). We port this toolkit wholesale to biological LLMs and treat 'how linear, how low-dimensional, how convergent' as measurable quantities.
What single-cell foundation models encode. SCFMs differ in tokenization and scale-rank-value encoding in Geneformer (Theodoris et al., 2023), binned-value tokens in scGPT (Cui et al., 2024) and scBERT (Yang et al., 2022), protein-embedding gene keys in UCE (Rosen et al., 2023), and cell-as-token modeling in CellPLM (Wen et al., 2024); reviews catalog the family (Szałata et al., 2024). Independent evaluations question the payoff of this scale (Boiarsky et al., 2023; Kedzierska et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023), and a mechanistic line finds organized-but-correlational content: co-expression-dominated attention (Kendiukhov, 2026b), interpretable cell-type programs but scarce regulatory logic in sparse-autoencoder features (Kendiukhov, 2026c,d), convergent inhibitory circuits (Kendiukhov, 2026a), a low-dimensional spectral geometry of knowledge (Kendiukhov, 2026e), and an extractable, curved hematopoietic manifold (Kendiukhov, 2026f). Our study is complementary and representational: rather than tracing circuits or dictionary features, we ask whether the geometry that makes LLM knowledge legible is present, and we benchmark it against expression baselines throughout.

Probing and its pitfalls. Linear classifier probes are the standard readout for 'is attribute u1D44B linearly present' (Alain and Bengio, 2016), but a probe's accuracy conflates the information in the representation with the capacity of the probe, so high accuracy need not imply the model uses or cleanly linearizes the attribute (Belinkov, 2022).
